title: Your Front Door Opens Before the Keys Hit the Counter
summary: Learn how collision repair shops can win customers before drop-off with faster response times, digital scheduling, AI, and a better customer experience.
body_markdown:
**By: Heidi Harris, Director, Solutions Engineer, CCC Intelligent Solutions**


Years ago, when I was running a shop's front office, I came in early one Monday and finally tackled our catch-all email inbox. Nobody really owned it. It was just there.


Buried in it were eleven weekend estimate requests, several with photos.


I spent the whole morning calling down the list. Two owners had decided not to fix the car. One went to the dealer. The rest had already booked somewhere else by Saturday afternoon. The woman I remember most was gracious about it. "Oh, honey, don't worry about it," she said. "Another shop texted me back Friday night, and they've already got the car."


That interaction stuck with me. If I hadn’t dug through that inbox, our weekly production reports would have simply read: "Quiet weekend." Today, at an average repair order of $4,000, we quietly surrendered roughly $30,000 in work before the front doors even unlocked on Monday. Those customers didn’t complain or leave negative reviews. They just vanished.


In a recent Run My Business episode, "[Win the Customer Before the Estimate Is Written](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m0kal9jekqo&list=PLujWGHP4XolojCh2N3mX9zggyHEF1v3GC&index=12) ," Craig Stevens makes the case that the first five minutes of drop-off set the tone for the whole repair. He’s spot on. I'd even start one step earlier, at the front door most of us leave unstaffed after 5:00 pm, the digital one.


## The first impression happens at the kitchen table


Craig points out that an anxious driver needs reassurance before they need an estimate. In my experience, that anxiety peaks the night of the accident, at the kitchen table with a phone in hand, long before the car shows up on your lot. And that driver is shopping harder than they used to. CCC's 2026 Crash Course report found affordability pressure is pushing consumers to treat lower-severity claims more like optional purchases. While BrightLocal’s 2026 survey also found that 97% of consumers now read reviews for local businesses.


So, by the time that customer walks up to your counter, they've already interviewed you. Your reviews, your website, your technology, and how fast you got back to them were the interview.


## Put your Laura on the digital front door


Craig tells a great story about Laura, a front desk manager whose notes about customers' lives turned into five-star reviews.


Every successful shop has a Laura. The problem is that most shops confine their Lauras behind the counter. While she’s charming walk-ins, online inquiries are routed into generic web forms, lists, or email boxes that are often the last thing someone checks for the day.


The digital equivalent of Laura’s handwritten note is a first response that sounds unmistakably human: a real name, acknowledgment of the stress they’re dealing with, and a painless next step.


"Hi Jennifer, this is Laura at Main Street Collision. I'm so sorry to hear about your accident. I received your photos of the bumper. We can definitely get that taken care of. Can you swing by Thursday at 8:30 AM to drop off your car and review the damage? We can have a rental lined up if you need one."


After hours, a well-tuned AI assistant can deliver a similar experience, letting Jennifer ask questions, upload photos, and book directly onto your shop calendar, all from her kitchen table.


## Use tech to educate before drop-off


Craig's tablet walk-around works because it shows instead of tells. You can establish that same transparency before they ever pull on to your lot.


Now, no estimator I know wants to write an estimate off blurry phone photos, and you don't have to. The point of online photo intake and self-scheduling is to give a stressed-out customer something to do tonight and a time on the calendar. It’s about reducing that customer’s anxiety and giving them some control back in a chaotic situation.


Take it a step further: use pre-repair confirmation texts to set expectations early:


- Explain why a pre-repair scan is non-negotiable for vehicle safety.
- Outline how parts delays or insurer approvals work.
- Explain the teardown process so supplemental damage isn't a shock later.


When an owner steps into your lobby already understanding OEM calibration and disassembly, the walk-around conversation begins with trust rather than suspicion.


## Put a clock on empathy


Craig's last point is that great shops train and measure empathy instead of leaving it to chance. On the digital side, empathy has a metric: response time.


When Harvard Business Review studied thousands of inbound business leads, companies that responded within an hour were nearly seven times more likely to qualify and win the business. In collision repair, after an accident, the shop that responds first with empathy wins the keys.


Now, you don't need anyone watching the inbox at 2:00 a.m., but you do need a standard.


- **During shop hours** : Assign an owner and contact every digital inquiry within 15–30 minutes.
- **After hours** : Let AI and self-scheduling keep the door open overnight but assign an owner to follow up within the first hour of opening the next morning.


Measure your response time weekly, and review lead conversion in your production meetings with the same urgency you give cycle time.


Your front counter will always be where trust is cemented. But the repair itself is often won at 9 p.m. on a cracked phone screen, by the shop whose digital front door stayed open, reassuring a stressed driver before anyone else even checked their inbox.


Watch Craig Stevens break down front-office excellence in this episode of the **Run My Business** series on CCC's YouTube channel:[Win the Customer Before the Estimate Is Written](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m0kal9jekqo&list=PLujWGHP4XolojCh2N3mX9zggyHEF1v3GC&index=12&utm_source=gemini)
